Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette:
Marisol had grown up in a Latin American household where she was supposed to be quiet, helpful, and grateful, and as a child she learned early that her caregiver's anger could arrive without warning. The abuse was physical and repeated, unfolding in the very spaces that should have felt ordinary and safe: a kitchen doorway, a hallway, the edge of a bed, the places where she had nowhere to move away. Decades later, when she tried to describe those years, she often struggled to make the story feel real even to herself. At times she could recall the facts with a flat, detached stillness, as if she were speaking about another girl entirely. She would say, almost apologetically, that it seemed impossible that such things had happened to her at all. At other moments, pieces of it would break in on her without invitation - a flash of a hand lifting, the hard look on a face, the feeling of bracing before impact - and then vanish just as quickly, leaving her disoriented and unsettled by how abruptly the past could intrude.

As an adult, Marisol built a life that valued order, usefulness, and physical competence. She became a physical therapist, a profession that allowed her to work carefully with bodies in pain while appearing composed and in control. In the clinic, she was known as steady and attentive, but she also found herself constantly scanning for ways to keep situations contained. She felt most comfortable when she could position herself with her back against a wall and a clear view of the room, especially in waiting areas or during staff meetings, where strangers or unfamiliar people could come up behind her. If someone approached her unexpectedly in an ordinary setting - a man stepping close in a grocery store aisle, a person moving toward her too quickly in the parking lot, a stranger coming near her in the clinic lobby - she would tense immediately and feel as though danger were already present, even when nothing overt had happened. Nights were no easier. She often woke in the dark and checked her surroundings before settling again, needing to make sure she was safe before she could sleep, then waking later to repeat the same ritual.

Over time, Marisol came to organize her days around reducing strain. She avoided anything that might become stressful, declining invitations, postponing calls, and narrowing her world whenever she could. At home, she cleaned and organized repeatedly, going back over the same counters, drawers, and closets until things looked precise enough to quiet her. The repetition gave her a temporary sense of control, as if if everything was in its place then perhaps nothing else could break in. When the unease lingered anyway, she ate excessively, especially in the evenings after work, not out of enjoyment so much as to blunt the intensity of what she was feeling. These habits gradually shaped her routines and relationships. She became less available socially, more private, and more reluctant to let the day carry any uncertainty into her home.

At work, the effects were especially apparent in the physical therapy clinic, where patients, coworkers, and visitors moved through the space in unpredictable ways. A new patient approaching too directly, someone appearing behind her in a hallway, or a crowded treatment room could make her feel cornered, and she would subtly change her position so that she could see everyone present. Even so, she kept functioning, relying on competence and routine to get through the day. What finally brought her in for help was the growing burden of living this way at 59, divorced and increasingly tired of arranging her life around fear that other people could not see. She was ashamed that even now a stranger's approach could set her nerves on edge, and she was worn down by the nightly checking, the repeated cleaning, and the overeating that left her feeling out of control. Marisol did not expect to forget what happened, but she wanted the memories to stop arriving as fragments and to stop feeling so unreal that she doubted her own history. More than anything, she wanted to feel safe in ordinary places - at work, in public, and in her own home - without always needing a wall at her back.
